blocks.text: A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a period of time. It protects a service from abuse (scrapers, credential stuffing), from accidental overload (a buggy client in a retry loop), and enforces business rules (100 requests/min on the free tier). It's also how you share a scarce resource fairly — one noisy tenant shouldn't starve everyone else.

Requests over the limit get rejected immediately with **HTTP 429 Too Many Requests**, ideally with headers telling the client when to retry. Rejecting early is far cheaper than doing the work and failing later.

head: Key (who is limited)
Example
rows: Protect a downstream dependency: 2,000 req/s total

blocks.caption: Rate limit as early as possible

blocks.text: Coarse limits at the edge stop floods before they reach your infrastructure; precise per-user limits live in the gateway, which can read the API key; and services can add concurrency limits around especially expensive operations.

**Token bucket.** Picture a bucket that holds up to `capacity` tokens and is refilled at `rate` tokens per second. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. A full bucket allows a burst of `capacity` requests, after which traffic is smoothed to `rate`. You don't need a timer to refill — compute the refill lazily from the elapsed time when a request arrives.

**Leaky bucket.** Requests join a FIFO queue that drains at a constant rate; if the queue is full, new requests are dropped. Output is perfectly smooth, which suits traffic shaping toward a fragile downstream, but bursts wait in line (adding latency) instead of being served immediately.

**Fixed window counter.** Count requests per key per calendar window (e.g. per minute: key `user:42:12:05`). Cheap — one INCR + EXPIRE — but at window boundaries a client can send the full limit at 12:05:59 and again at 12:06:00: **2× the limit in two seconds**.

**Sliding window log.** Store a timestamp per request (Redis sorted set), drop ones older than the window, count the rest. Exact, but memory grows with the limit (a 10k/hour limit stores 10k entries per user).

**Sliding window counter.** Keep counts for the current and previous fixed windows and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window: `estimate = prev × (1 − elapsed/window) + current`. It's a near-exact approximation with two counters per key — the usual production choice alongside token bucket.

sections.title: Making it work across many gateways

blocks.text: With 50 gateway instances, each one can't keep its own counter — a user would get 50× the limit. The counter has to be shared, and the check-and-increment must be **atomic**, or two instances will both read 99, both allow, and both write 100.

blocks.caption: Atomic check-and-consume in Redis (one round trip)

blocks.text:
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key, ARGV = rate, capacity, now_ms
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local rate, cap, now = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)
local allowed = tokens >= 1
if allowed then tokens = tokens - 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000))
return { allowed and 1 or 0, math.floor(tokens) }

items: **Shard Redis by limit key** (Redis Cluster hashes keys to slots) so throughput scales with nodes.

**Latency budget:** one Redis round trip (~0.5–1 ms in-region) per request. For extreme QPS, keep a small local token allowance per instance and sync with Redis in batches — slightly less accurate, far fewer calls.
**Clock source:** use Redis server time (`TIME`) or the caller's clock consistently, so instances with skewed clocks don't disagree.

sections.title: Failure modes and choices you must make

cols.title: Fail open (allow when Redis is down)
cons: No protection during the outage — the moment you may need it most

cols.title: Fail closed (reject when Redis is down)
cons: Your limiter outage becomes a full outage

items: Most public APIs **fail open** with a conservative per-instance local limit as a fallback.
Hot keys: one enormous tenant concentrates load on a single Redis shard — split its key (`tenant:7#0..7`) and divide the limit.
Multi-region: either per-region limits (simple, slightly generous) or asynchronously replicated counters (eventually consistent).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Implementing the limit as GET, compare, then SET from the application. Without atomicity (Lua script, INCR, or MULTI), concurrent requests race and the limit leaks.

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 12

items: Return `Retry-After` so well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering.
Clients should retry with **exponential backoff + jitter**; otherwise thousands of clients retry in lockstep.
Return remaining-quota headers on successful responses too, so clients can pace themselves.
Log and meter rejections per key — they're a product signal (who needs a higher plan) and a security signal.

sections.title: Beyond request counts: adaptive limits and load shedding

blocks.text: Fixed limits protect against misbehaving clients, but not against your own capacity dropping (a slow database, a bad deploy). **Adaptive concurrency limits** (e.g. Netflix's concurrency-limits library, based on TCP congestion control) watch latency and shrink the number of in-flight requests when latency rises.

items: **Load shedding by priority:** under pressure, drop low-priority traffic (analytics, prefetch) first and keep checkout working.
**Concurrency limits** (max in-flight requests) are often better than rate limits for expensive endpoints, because cost varies per request.
**Cost-based limits:** charge different token amounts per operation (a search costs 10 tokens, a read costs 1) — GitHub's GraphQL API does this with query cost points.

sections.title: Putting it together in an interview

items.title: Clarify
items.text: Who is limited (user, IP, tenant)? Hard or soft limits? Single region or global?

items.title: Pick an algorithm
items.text: Token bucket if bursts are fine; sliding window counter if limits must be even.

items.title: Place it
items.text: Edge for IP floods, gateway for API keys, service for concurrency.

items.title: Make it distributed
items.text: Redis + Lua for atomic check-and-consume, sharded by key.

items.title: Handle failure
items.text: Fail open with local fallback; 429 + Retry-After; client backoff with jitter.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd run a token bucket per API key in Redis, executed as a Lua script so refill-and-consume is atomic, sharded by key, failing open to a local limit if Redis is unavailable, and returning 429 with Retry-After.
